opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important and underrated questions. There's a picture where once you have really capable AI systems, everything just speeds up uniformly: you have millions of brilliant researchers running at many times human speed, and problems melt away. I think that's roughly right for things that live mostly in the world of bits, like writing software, doing math, or analyzing existing data. But many of the defense and policy problems we care about are bottlenecked by things that don't speed up just because cognition gets cheaper.

The most obvious one is physical experimentation and manufacturing. Take biodefense. If you want better PPE, better air filtration, far-UVC deployed in buildings, or broad-spectrum countermeasures, AI can help a lot with the design. But at some point you have to grow the cells, run the assays, do animal studies, and build the factories. Wet lab work has its own clock speed. Cultures take the time they take. Clinical trials are partly bottlenecked by regulation, but also by needing to watch what happens to people over months. Automated labs and better simulation can compress some of that, but probably not by the factors we'd see on the purely cognitive side.

The second category is deployment and adoption. Even if you have a great solution on paper, you need it physically installed across millions of buildings, or hardened into critical infrastructure, or integrated into power grids and water systems. That means procurement cycles, supply chains, permits, and workforce training. Those are slow for reasons that have very little to do with how smart anyone is.

Then there's the policy side, where I think the bottleneck is human deliberation and legitimacy. AI could draft excellent legislation or model the consequences of different regulatory regimes in a fraction of the time. But you still need legislators to understand it, stakeholders to weigh in, courts to interpret it, and the public to accept it. You don't want to fully compress that, because a lot of its value comes from humans actually buying in. And international coordination, like treaties or verification regimes, is slower still, because you need trust built between parties who have reasons to be suspicious of each other.

So the worry is a mismatch in speeds. Offensive capabilities, or the general capability frontier, could advance at software speed, while our defenses advance at hardware, bureaucracy, and diplomacy speed. That gap is where a lot of the risk lives.

The practical upshot for me is that we should start the slow stuff now, before we have the transformative systems. Build manufacturing capacity, stockpile countermeasures, lay the groundwork for institutions and verification mechanisms, and get regulators fluent in this technology. Those are the long-lead-time items. If you wait until AI is good enough to design the solutions and only then start the physical and political processes, you may find the clock has already run out.

r001.rationale: The response identifies human deliberation, buy-in, and trust as policy bottlenecks, but it does not clearly connect them to policymaking between the US and China.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the bottlenecks look pretty different depending on which of those two buckets you're in, and it's worth separating them.

On the physical side, the thing I keep coming back to is that cognition has gotten cheap and fast, but the world hasn't. If you want to, say, build better air defense or harden the grid or develop broad-spectrum countermeasures for a bio threat, you can have the AI design the thing in an afternoon, but then you have to actually make it. You have to run the experiments, you have to wait for the clinical trial to read out, you have to get the components manufactured, you have to pour the concrete. A lot of that is bound by processes that just take the amount of time they take. Cells grow at a certain rate. Supply chains have lead times. And I think people who've spent their careers in software systematically underestimate this, because in software you can iterate a thousand times a day. So my expectation is that the physical defense problems will be gated much more by how fast you can run the loop of build, test, learn in the real world than by how smart the AI is. The AI can compress the design step enormously, but then you hit this wall of atoms moving around.

Now, I don't think that's totally fixed. One of the interesting things about having a lot of AI labor is you can parallelize experiments in ways that were previously too expensive, you can run way more simulations before you touch the physical world, you can automate a lot of lab work. So I'd expect the wall to move. But it moves slower than the cognitive side, and that gap is where a lot of the danger lives, honestly, because offense in some domains may need less physical iteration than defense does.

The policy side is almost the opposite problem. There, the bottleneck is less about physics and more about humans and institutions. You could have an AI system that produces a genuinely excellent proposal for how to govern compute or how to structure international verification, and that proposal then has to go through people. It has to be understood by staffers, it has to survive a committee, it has to be negotiated between countries that don't trust each other. And those processes run at the speed of human attention and human trust-building, which is really slow. Elections are on fixed schedules. Legislative sessions are on fixed schedules. Treaties take years. None of that gets faster just because the analysis got faster.

And there's a subtler version of the problem, which is legitimacy. Even if the AI's recommendation is right, people need time to feel like they've actually deliberated about it, like it's their decision. If you shortcut that, you might get the right policy on paper and then have it collapse because nobody feels ownership of it. So I actually think some of the time cost in policy is not waste, it's doing real work. It's what makes the outcome stick.

So if you ask me where I'm most worried, it's actually the mismatch. We're going to have a world where the number of good ideas being generated goes up by orders of magnitude, and the institutions that have to absorb and act on those ideas are still moving at roughly the pace they do today. The question I think about is less "how do we make the AI better" and more "how do we build institutions and physical infrastructure that can metabolize this faster without breaking." That might mean pre-committing to certain response procedures ahead of time, building up manufacturing capacity for things we think we'll need before we know exactly what they are, that sort of thing. Basically front-loading the slow stuff so we're not starting from zero when the fast stuff arrives.

r001.rationale: The response identifies slow human negotiation, trust-building, and deliberation as policy bottlenecks, but it discusses countries generally and never identifies US–China policymaking or an agreement between those countries.

astra-6.text:
I’d expect the bottlenecks to shift toward things where you have to wait for the physical world or for people. An AI might come up with a promising defense very quickly, but then you still have to test it, manufacture it, deploy it, and figure out whether it actually works under realistic conditions. You can speed up some of that with better reasoning and simulation, but you can’t necessarily compress the whole process to the speed of thought.

And on the policy side, having a good proposal is different from getting it adopted. People need to understand it, negotiate over it, and decide whom to trust. There may be genuinely conflicting interests that more intelligence doesn’t just dissolve.

So I’d distinguish between the time to figure out what to do and the time to make it happen. AI could dramatically shorten the first while leaving substantial bottlenecks in the second. That’s especially concerning if creating a new threat requires fewer physical steps or fewer people’s cooperation than putting a defense in place.

r001.rationale: The response says policy proposals may be delayed while people understand, negotiate, and decide whom to trust, but it does not identify US–China policymaking.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d expect a lot of the bottlenecks to be in getting feedback from the world. An AI might be able to generate a design or a policy proposal very quickly, but that doesn’t mean you can quickly establish that it works. For a physical defense, you may need to manufacture something, test it under realistic conditions, and then build enough of it to deploy. Those steps can take time even if the intellectual work becomes much faster.

And with policy, there’s an additional problem: people have to understand the proposal, trust the evidence, negotiate, and actually implement it. If you’re proposing a major change, the fact that an AI can produce a very compelling analysis in an afternoon doesn’t necessarily make the institutions move in an afternoon.

So I’d distinguish between having an answer that looks good and having a solution that’s been validated and put into practice. AI could accelerate all of those stages, but I wouldn’t assume they accelerate at the same rate. The slowest parts may be experiments, production, and human coordination.

r001.rationale: The response describes human understanding, trust, negotiation, and institutional implementation as slow parts of policymaking. It does not identify US–China policymaking or clearly state that decision-makers need time to reach an agreement they endorse.
